subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which parts of the UK are mainly upland and mountainous?
options: The north and west
The south and east
The central lowlands only
The coastal areas only
questions.explain: The UK's higher, more rugged upland relief is concentrated in the north and west, while lowlands dominate the south and east.

questions.q: Which of these is a characteristic of a constructive wave?
options: A strong swash and weak backwash
A weak swash and strong backwash
A high, steep wave form
A high frequency of 10-14 waves per minute
questions.explain: Constructive waves have a strong swash and weak backwash, so they build up beaches through deposition.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly shows the formation of a stack from a headland?
options: Crack → cave → arch → stack → stump
Cave → crack → stack → arch → stump
Arch → cave → crack → stump → stack
Stump → stack → arch → cave → crack
questions.explain: Erosion widens a crack into a cave, then an arch, which collapses to leave a stack that is later eroded to a stump.

questions.q: Which statement best describes hydraulic power as a process of coastal erosion?
options: The force of water compressing air in cracks in the rock
Rocks carried by waves scraping against the cliff face
Pebbles being worn down as they collide with each other
Weak acids in seawater dissolving the rock
questions.explain: Hydraulic power is the force of waves forcing water and compressed air into cracks, weakening and breaking the rock.

questions.q: The direction in which longshore drift transports sediment along a coast is mainly controlled by:
options: The prevailing wind direction
The gravitational pull of the moon
The gradient of the sea bed only
The type of rock forming the cliff
questions.explain: The prevailing wind drives the swash up the beach at an angle, so it sets the overall direction of longshore drift.

questions.q: A spit is most likely to form where:
options: The coastline changes direction and sediment is deposited across a gap
Two headlands are eroded to form a bay between them
A river deepens its channel by vertical erosion
Waves refract around a resistant headland
questions.explain: Where the coastline bends, longshore drift continues to deposit sediment out into open water, building an elongated spit.

questions.q: A seaside town finds its beach is shrinking as sand is carried away along the coast. Which strategy would most directly trap sediment and rebuild the beach?
options: Building groynes
Building a sea wall
Adopting managed retreat
Removing vegetation from the cliff top
questions.explain: Groynes are wooden or rock barriers built at right angles to the coast that trap sediment moving by longshore drift, widening the beach.

questions.q: In the upper course of a river, the dominant type of erosion is:
options: Vertical erosion
Lateral erosion
Deposition
Coastal erosion
questions.explain: In the upper course the river cuts downwards through vertical erosion, creating steep-sided, V-shaped valleys.

questions.q: A gorge is found downstream of a waterfall because:
options: The waterfall retreats upstream as the overhanging rock collapses
Lateral erosion widens the valley floor over time
Deposition builds up the bed of the river
A meander has been abandoned by the river
questions.explain: Undercutting causes the overhang to collapse, so the waterfall retreats upstream and leaves a steep-sided gorge behind it.

questions.q: An ox-bow lake is formed when:
options: Erosion narrows a meander neck until the river cuts across it and deposition seals it off
A river deposits its coarsest load to form a natural embankment
Bands of hard and soft rock are eroded at different rates
A glacier deepens and straightens a former river valley
questions.explain: Erosion on the outer bends narrows the meander neck until the river breaks through, then deposition cuts off the loop as an ox-bow lake.

questions.q: Levees are natural raised banks that form when:
options: A river floods and deposits its coarsest load on the banks
A meander is cut off from the main channel
Vertical erosion deepens the river channel
Waves deposit sediment along a beach
questions.explain: During a flood the river loses energy at its banks and drops the heaviest sediment first, building up raised levees over time.

questions.q: River discharge is measured in:
options: Cumecs (cubic metres per second)
Metres per second
Millimetres per hour
Kilometres squared
questions.explain: Discharge is the volume of water passing a point per second, measured in cumecs (cubic metres per second).

questions.q: On a flood (storm) hydrograph, lag time is:
options: The time between peak rainfall and peak discharge
The total length of time that rain falls
The time taken for the river to return to base flow
The height reached by the peak discharge
questions.explain: Lag time is the delay between the peak of rainfall and the peak discharge of the river.

questions.q: A drainage basin has impermeable clay geology, steep slopes and heavy rainfall. The most likely effect on flood risk is:
options: Increased flood risk because surface run-off is rapid
Reduced flood risk because water infiltrates quickly
No change to the flood risk of the basin
Increased infiltration and a much longer lag time
questions.explain: Impermeable rock and steep slopes reduce infiltration and speed up surface run-off, shortening lag time and raising flood risk.

questions.q: A corrie (cirque) is best described as:
options: An armchair-shaped hollow with a steep back wall
A knife-edged ridge between two valleys
A pointed mountain summit
A long, deep U-shaped valley
questions.explain: A corrie is a deep, armchair-shaped hollow eroded by ice, with a steep back wall and often a small lake (tarn).

questions.q: A pyramidal peak forms where:
options: Three or more corries erode back to back around a mountain
A glacier deposits moraine at its snout
A ribbon lake fills a glacial trough
Two glaciers merge to form medial moraine
questions.explain: When three or more corries erode backwards around the same mountain, the remaining central summit becomes a sharp pyramidal peak.

questions.q: Plucking is a process of glacial erosion in which:
options: Ice freezes onto rock and pulls fragments away as the glacier moves
Rock fragments in the ice scrape and smooth the valley floor
Meltwater dissolves the underlying rock
The glacier slides forward on a layer of meltwater
questions.explain: In plucking, meltwater freezes onto rock and, as the glacier moves, it tears loose fragments away from the bedrock.

questions.q: A glacial trough differs from a river valley because it is typically:
options: U-shaped with a wide, flat floor and steep sides
V-shaped with interlocking spurs
Shallow with a gentle gradient throughout
Formed entirely by deposition
questions.explain: Glaciers erode valleys into a wide, steep-sided U-shape, unlike the V-shaped valleys carved by rivers.

questions.q: A stretch of low-value farmland behind eroding cliffs is deliberately allowed to flood and revert to salt marsh. This management approach is:
options: Managed retreat (coastal realignment)
Rock armour
Beach nourishment
Channel straightening
questions.explain: Managed retreat allows low-value land to flood, creating natural salt marsh that absorbs wave energy at low cost.

questions.q: After a drainage basin is urbanised and covered in concrete, its storm hydrograph is most likely to show:
options: A shorter lag time and higher peak discharge
A longer lag time and lower peak discharge
No peak discharge at all
A lower and much later peak discharge
questions.explain: Impermeable concrete and drains speed run-off into the river, shortening lag time and increasing peak discharge and flood risk.
